fields.description:
TaskMemoryManager adds a consumer to its consumers set on every acquireExecutionMemory call, but nothing removes it before cleanUpAllAllocatedMemory() at the end of the task. A consumer that has released all its memory (or has been closed) therefore stays reachable until the task ends, together with everything it references, and both spill loops (acquireExecutionMemory and spillConsumersForPageAllocation) keep scanning it on every spill.

This was raised in the review of SPARK-60112 (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59331#discussion_r4236874042). After SPARK-60112 tracks consumers by identity, equal-but-distinct consumers that used to be collapsed into a single entry are each retained this way, although the same already holds for any other distinct consumer.

Proposal: drop a consumer from the set once it no longer holds memory (for example when its usage reaches zero, or when it is closed), instead of only ever adding to it.
fields.summary: Remove memory consumers from TaskMemoryManager once they no longer hold memory

fields.description:
Follow-up of SPARK-60119, which bounds the rescaling in `Decimal.changePrecision`.

`Decimal.set(decimal: BigDecimal, precision: Int, scale: Int)` still calls `decimal.setScale(scale, ROUND_HALF_UP)` without bounding the scale change. It is used by the JSON, CSV and XML parsers for decimal fields (`JacksonParser`, `UnivocityParser`, `StaxXmlParser`), and also by Avro, JDBC and `ToNumberParser`. With a `DECIMAL(10,2)` schema:

- `from_json('{"a": 1e-2147483647}', 'a DECIMAL(10,2)')` and `from_csv('1e-2147483647', 'a DECIMAL(10,2)')` fail with `ArithmeticException: BigInteger would overflow supported range`, so the record is treated as malformed (null in PERMISSIVE, error in FAILFAST), while `1e-10000000` correctly gives 0.00.
- `1e-10000000` takes ~1.4s per value and `1e10000000` ~5s per value; exponents around 1e8 take ~40s per value.

Overflow in this method is reported as `NUMERIC_VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE.WITHOUT_SUGGESTION` with a `roundedValue`, so the large side needs a decision on what to report without computing the rounded value.

`Decimal.set(decimal: BigDecimal)` has a similar issue: with `spark.sql.legacy.allowNegativeScaleOfDecimal=false` it calls `decimal.setScale(0)` for a negative scale, which fails for e.g. a `java.math.BigDecimal("1e2147483647")` coming from a non-string input. The string cast path is guarded by the fast-fail in `Decimal.fromString` (see SPARK-60118).
fields.summary: Decimal.set fails or is slow when the value scale is far from the target scale
Casting a string with an exponent near Int.MaxValue to decimal throws ArithmeticException instead of NULL / NUMERIC_OUT_OF_SUPPORTED_RANGE

fields.description:
SPARK-60118 bounds the number of integral digits (precision - scale, now computed in Long) only in Decimal.fromString / fromStringANSI, i.e. the string-to-decimal cast path. Other entry points that build a Decimal from a BigDecimal have no such bound and can still fail with a raw java.lang.ArithmeticException (or spend a long time in BigDecimal.setScale) for values with a huge exponent:

* Decimal.set(BigDecimal) computes this._precision = decimal.precision - decimal.scale as an Int, which overflows for e.g. 1e2147483647 or 0e2147483647, and then calls decimal.setScale(0). Decimal(String) and Decimal(java.math.BigDecimal) go through this.
* Decimal.set(BigDecimal, precision, scale), used by Decimal(bd, precision, scale), calls decimal.setScale(scale) directly. The CSV reader (UnivocityParser) and the JSON reader (JacksonParser) use it for decimal columns. There the exception is currently turned into a bad record (or a failure in FAILFAST mode) rather than a NULL field.

Suggested direction: move the Long-based integral-digit bound into Decimal.set or a shared helper, so these paths don't depend on the string-cast fast path.

Reported in the review of https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59334.
fields.summary: Bound the integral-digit count of BigDecimal values in Decimal.set to avoid raw ArithmeticException for huge exponents

fields.description:
Problem

In the Scala Spark Connect client, removing a streaming listener that was never registered can stop event delivery for another registered listener. The removal code checks whether one listener remains, but does not check whether it is removing that listener before stopping the shared bus.

How to reproduce

1. Register listener A with spark.streams.addListener(A).
2. Call spark.streams.removeListener(B), where B is a different listener that was never registered.
3. The client sends a command to remove the shared server-side listener bus and interrupts its event worker.

Expected behavior

Removing B should do nothing. Listener A should remain registered and continue receiving events. This also matches the membership check already used by Python Connect.

Why this fix is needed

Removing an unrelated listener should not disable event handling for a registered listener. The server cannot prevent this mistake because the removal command addresses the shared bus, rather than an individual client listener.

Proposed change and testing

Check that the listener is registered before stopping the shared bus. Keep the existing behavior for removing a registered listener, including the last listener.

A focused test against the production removal method fails before the fix because it records an unwanted bus removal command. After the fix, that test, the registered-listener removal test, and SparkSessionSuite pass: 12 tests in total. Module style checks also pass. The existing live-server streaming listener test also fails before the fix because the termination event is not delivered, and passes after the fix. It checks progress and termination events for both listener interface variants. No tests were ignored in either live run.

Related issues

SPARK-59847 and SPARK-59623 concern Python Connect deadlocks when removing the last registered listener. This issue concerns removing an unregistered listener in the Scala client, so the trigger and fix are different.

SPARK-58000 concerns Scala listener-test flakiness caused by interrupted worker cleanup. It is related lifecycle context, but does not address this missing membership check.

Affected versions

The same removal path is present in the Spark 4.0.0 source. The regression was run on the current 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT master checkout; no released-version runtime test was run.
fields.summary: Removing an unregistered Scala Connect streaming listener stops the shared bus

items.fromString:
In the Scala Spark Connect client, removing a StreamingQueryListener that was never registered can unregister the shared server-side listener bus when exactly one other listener is registered.

Reproduction sequence:
1. Add listener A with spark.streams.addListener(A).
2. Call spark.streams.removeListener(B), where B is a different listener that was never added.
3. StreamingQueryListenerBus.remove sees one registration and sends remove_listener_bus_listener=true before checking membership. It also interrupts the event worker. Removing B from the local list does not remove A.

Expected: removing B is a no-op and A keeps its registration and event handling.
Actual: the client sends the command that unregisters the shared server-side bus and interrupts the worker. Later local state depends on whether the worker completes normally or enters its exception cleanup path.

A deterministic regression against the production Scala remove method at upstream/master commit 215a1460d9d4acdac6f72b42c28ab60b9ff5b7fe fails because an unregister command is recorded for B. The registered-listener removal case passes. The fixture substitutes remote command execution and worker input; this is not a live-server reproduction.

Python Connect already checks listener membership before unregistering the bus. SPARK-59847 and SPARK-59623 concern Python worker-join deadlocks and do not change the Scala membership check.

Proposed fix: require listeners.contains(listener) in the existing single-listener unregister condition. No API, protocol, duplicate-registration, or threading-policy change.
